title: Spark's Satellite Secret
markdown:
Dawn broke. Gold streaked the window. Mina woke with a happy buzz in her chest. Today felt different. Special.

Her foxy pal Flint skittered in, ears perked.

“Mina! Big trouble!”

Mina’s heart thumped. “What?”

“Spark is gone!”

Spark, her drone. Her science-fair centrepiece. Gone? Impossible. She dashed to the workshop. The launchpad stood empty. A cold knot tightened in her stomach.

Professor Imani bustled in, coat flapping like a flag in a hurry. “Spark? Oh, dear Mina. We need him for the solar demonstration. The fair depends on him capturing sunlight from way up high.”

Mina grabbed Spark’s data log. Her fingers flew. Last known coordinates. Beeps. Static. Scrambled data. Nothing. Flint nudged her, worried. Professor Imani peered at the screen.

“Look at these transmission timestamps,” she said. “Notice the precise timed pulses.”

Mina zoomed in. Tiny consistent gaps. Like cosmic clock ticks.

“They’re like clocks ticking,” she whispered. Understanding zipped through her.

“Exactly.” Professor Imani’s eyes sparked. “Satellites do this. Their signals tell us distance. Knowing satellite locations and signal times pinpoints our location. It’s called trilateration: a mathematical treasure hunt.”

Mina’s mind raced. Timing signals. Distances. Geometry.

“So if Spark sent signals,” she began, voice picking up speed, “and we know when he sent them…”

“We can calculate where he is!” Flint yipped, bouncing. His tail thumped.

Professor Imani grabbed a calculator and patted it as if it were a trustworthy hound. “This uses geometry to map distances by signal delay. Input the timings. Let’s see what Spark was telling us.”

Mina typed. Flint watched, nose nearly on the keys. The calculator whirred. Numbers flashed.

“It says…” Mina gasped. “Blackwood Creek. Miles away. Far beyond his usual flight path.”

“But how did he get there?” Flint asked.

“A strong gust, perhaps,” Professor Imani said. “But the timing signals were his way of calling out. They guided us, just as they guide ships and planes.”

They packed a backpack. With Flint sniffing the air, they hopped on their bikes. Cool morning air whipped past. Dew flashed on the hedgerows. They raced toward Blackwood Creek.

Soon they heard babbling water. There, on a mossy bank, sat Spark. His camera pointed skyward. He was unharmed.

Mina scooped him up, relief flooding her. “You clever drone. You told us where you were.”

Spark’s casing was cool from the creek-shadow. The solar demo was safe. A whole geometry of distant pulses had been waiting in the log the whole time, if you knew how to listen.

Flint puffed his chest and barked as if he had invented maths.

Mina clipped Spark back into his harness, already thinking of other clocks ticking in the sky. The fair still waited. The day was only getting started.

“Today,” she declared, “is going to be amazing.”
characters: Mina (an observant coder), Flint (a perked-eared fox), Professor Imani (a solar-fair teacher)
